newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico economy on the mend, but is consumer?.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico economy on the mend, but is consumer?.

text.p: Mexico's economy bounced back better than expected last year from the devastating peso crisis, but economists are not yet sure about the fate of the final and most critical piece of the recovery: the consumer.

Mexico's economy grew 5.1 percent in 1996, the Finance Ministry said on Wednesday -- far above expectations of about 4.5 percent yearly growth. During the fourth quarter alone, the economy grew a suprisingly strong 7.6 percent.
The return to growth was welcome news in a country that had suffered an economic decline of 6.2 percent in 1995, its worst recession since the Great Depression.
"There is no denying 1996 was a bounce-back year for Mexico," James Carlen, director of economic research on emerging markets at American Express Financial Services, told Reuters.
"The GDP number on the face of it is very positive...But I think that a really important part of growth, the consumer, is not yet contributing."

For most of the year, strong growth in manufacturing and construction carried the economy amid evidence that the consumer was still suffering under a mountain of debt and not yet close to spending as much as before the peso crash.

But in the fourth quarter, most of the growth came from the services sector, which rose 10.1 percent compared to the same period of 1995. Services include areas such as commercial establishments and restaurants that are a good indicator of consumer spending, economists said.

"The manufacturing and construction story in Mexico is old. What we wanted to see was the growth in manufacturing and construction spread to the service sector. Now it seems the recovery is generalized," said Lawrence Krohn, head of Latin America economic and equity research at UBS Securities.

Krohn and others added, however, that aggregate demand numbers due out in a few weeks would give a clearer picture of what accounted for the growth in demand. On Thursday, retail sales figures for November and December are also due.
What still troubled some economists despite the positive numbers is the lack of other signs in the economy that consumption is on the mend.

Retail sales in Mexico have continued to be sluggish. In October, retail sales rose just 2.1 percent compared to the same month a year earlier. Some corporate earnings have also shown weak revenues during the fourth quarter.

And Mexican households still have a net outflow of credit to banks, meaning they are paying more debt than they are receiving in new credit, according to Denis Parisien, an analyst at Bankers Trust in New York.

Government officials said on Wednesday that they were also puzzled by the mixed evidence and suggested the rise in the service sector could have largely come from a recovery in the informal economy -- Mexico's millions who eke out a living as street vendors.
But they also said they have seen signs of a rebound in consumption such as an increase in credit card spending and employment in the service sector.

"We do have other important indicators that consumption is registering increases.... We think these numbers are showing important, or at least considerable, increases in the second part of 1996 compared to the first part of 1996," a high-ranking finance ministry official told analysts during a conference call.
Parisien suggested some of the difference could be accounted for by Mexico's growing trade sector -- which could be having a collateral effect on consumption.
